new_statements.quote: p.155: "Stress assignment in Salar. Salar, like other Turkic languages, is commonly said to have fixed word-ultimate stress (see e.g. Lín 1985). While some kind of ultimate stress can be posited as a default setting, stress assignment in ..." p.156: "derivational suffixes surfacing in non-final position override Final Stress and are assigned stress" p.160: "a minority of morphemes are never stressed when occurring in ultimate position" p.162: "This stress-attraction varies considerably from speaker to speaker, however. Occasionally, such stress distinctions are distinctive. The Eastern Salar necessitative /geler/, which receives default final stress, is ..." p.84: "Western Salar does not have any initial stress."
new_statements.citation: Dwyer, Arienne M. 2007. Salar: A Study in Inner Asian Language Contact Processes. Part I: Phonology (Turcologica 37.1). Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz.
new_statements.locator: §5.7.1 'Stress assignment in Salar', p. 155 (opening sentences); supplementary fragments pp. 156, 160, 162 and pp. 83-84 (dialect criteria)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default (unmarked) word stress is on the final syllable, as traditionally claimed for Salar and for Turkic generally; Dwyer treats this only as a default, overridden by morpheme-based factors: certain derivational suffixes (e.g. denominal -lA/-rA) attract stress even in non-final position, a minority of suffixes (some nominal suffixes such as plural -lAr in some contexts, and other 'unstressed suffixes', §5.8) never take stress even when word-final, so stress then falls on the preceding syllable; syllable weight plays only an occasional role; some trisyllabic stems and some Qinghai (Eastern Salar) varieties show initial stress under Chinese influence, which Western (Ili) Salar lacks.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the snippets retrieved.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress-attracting derivational suffixes in non-final position; unstressed morphemes in final position; occasional weight-sensitivity; Arabic/Persian and Tibetan loans with special stress features; initial stress in some trisyllabic stems and in some Eastern Salar (Qinghai) varieties with 'considerable' speaker-to-speaker variation; stress occasionally distinctive (e.g. necessitative vs. a form with non-final stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in the phonological word (stem + suffixes); Dwyer 2007 covers both Eastern Salar (Xunhua/Hualong, Qinghai; Jishishan, Gansu) and Western/Ili Salar (Xinjiang). The quote is assembled from Google Books search-inside snippets (partial preview); the p.155 sentence is cut off after 'stress assignment in' and the full pages 155-162 were not obtained.
new_statements.identity_note: Dwyer 2007 describes Salar as a whole (glottocode sala1264) with two main varieties: Eastern Salar (Xunhua and Hualong counties, Qinghai; Jishishan, Gansu) and Western/Ili Salar (Xinjiang). The default final-stress statement applies to both; the initial-stress deviations are regional within Eastern Salar in Qinghai (Chinese influence), and Dwyer states explicitly that Western Salar has no initial stress. No separate glottocodes for the dialects in Glottolog 5.1's list seen here.

sources.note: No phonology chapter and no stress statement; refers to Dwyer (2007) for phonology ('Elle traite également de la prosodie', p.126) and only reports Dwyer's remark that unstressed-syllable vowel reductions may come from Tibetan contact (p.117). §4.1.3 pp.125-127 reviews all Salar descriptions (Tenishev 1976 has phonetics/phonology + morphology; Mehmet 2012 has a phonology part; Lin & Han 1962, Lin 1985/1986, Han 1988-1990 give 'éléments généraux de phonologie').

sources.citation: Poppe, Nicholas. 1953. Remarks on the Salar Language. Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies 16(3/4): 438-477. DOI 10.2307/2718250.
sources.note: Silent on stress placement (historical-comparative phonology based on Potanin's 1893 wordlist). Only a passing remark p.450: 'It is possible, however, that the gemination is connected somehow with the accent' (re -kk- in numerals in other Turkic languages).

sources.note: Morphology thesis; no general stress rule.
